# v6

**Fixed: listing the registered OPC servers crashed the helper on machines that
have classic OPC installed.**

The helper asked Windows for the OPC server-list object, then used the answer as
if it were a different kind of object and called through it — an access violation
that killed it silently, with no message to show. It only happened where classic
OPC (OPCEnum) is actually registered: everywhere else the request fails first and
the tool correctly reported "no classic OPC here", which is why this went unseen.

helper already did.

## v13.6

**Work it out for me pairs what the comparison pairs.** The proposal was built from the raw
top-level names, and the comparison does not match on those: it first expands every composite
definition into one entry per use and looks each one up by *classifier : name*. So the
auto-map was fed dozens of generated composite names (`__62B069D2_5F4D7CF0__`) that no rule
can pair, and it let a phase class pair with a unit class that merely shared a name -- which
is how it proposed `XFR -> A` on a trainee export. It now works from the comparison's own
keys, and a name pairs only with the same name of the same kind.

On TRAINING against TRAINING_A the proposal went from one rule pairing 150 names to a map
pairing 215 of 228 (222 of 228 the other way round); what is left is two classes the trainee
genuinely renamed.

- **Least difference breaks a tie.** Two rules that pair equally many names are decided by
  which one's pairs differ least in parameter content, then by which replacement looks most
  like its find. Without it, `_SETUP_A -> _XFR` -- a swap, same kind, same children -- could
  win over `_SETUP_A -> _SETUP`.
- **Small patterns and single renames.** A suffix carried by only two names (`_XFR`) is
  found on a second, relaxed pass, and a name renamed on its own (`AGITATE -> AGITATE_A`,
  `TRAINING -> TRAINING_A`) gets a whole-name rule.
- **Names the map would break are protected.** `_BA -> _A` also rewrites `_JKT_SEQ_EM_BA`,
  which is the same in both files; an identity rule keeps it paired, and keeps every
  reference to it from reading as a parameter difference.
- The proposal takes well under a second on the training pair (it took up to 30).

A frozen transmitter could be tuned as if it were a real response

Live logging read PV, OUT and SP with asyncua's `read_value()`, which returns the
value and throws the StatusCode away. A Bad, stale or frozen reading therefore
entered the dataset indistinguishable from live data — and a frozen transmitter
produces a clean, flat, entirely plausible response that the identifier fits
happily, handing back tuning constants for a loop that was never observed.

Reads now use the full DataValue and keep the quality:

- Logged samples carry a Quality flag (set when both PV and OUT came back Good).
  The status line warns the first time either goes not-good.
- Model fitting and the four-model competition refuse a window containing
  not-good samples, explaining why and asking before proceeding anyway.
- The step test aborts if OUT is not-good on the baseline read. Every step is
  measured against that number, so a bad baseline invalidates the whole test.
- CSV imports are taken at face value (Quality = good); the guard only ever
  fires on live-logged data.

# v5
Historian export comparator -- new `compare` CLI verb, no DeltaV connection needed

DvHistExport is no longer connection-only. `app.py` is now the built entry point
(`build.ps1`'s `-Entry "app"`): a `compare` verb on the command line runs headless,
before Tk or pythonnet/the DeltaV DLLs are even imported. No verb still opens the
window exactly as before, and `--selftest` is unchanged.

`DvHistExport.exe compare SOURCE.csv TARGET.csv --out REPORT.xlsx` compares two
historian exports (e.g. this tool's own "Export CSV..." output against a PI or
dataPARC export) for value/quality/timestamp agreement, matching samples within a
configurable time tolerance rather than requiring identical timestamps. It samples
`ceil(sqrt(N)) + 1` tags out of the total configured -- the same formula a real
Cornerstone dataPARC IQ/OQ deliverable uses to verify ongoing collection by hand
(72 of a 5000-tag system) -- chosen by even stride across the sorted tag list so
the sample is reproducible from the tag list alone. Writes a Sample Selection /
Comparison Evidence / Summary workbook. The comparison engine (`shared.histcompare`)
is shared with FHXport's new `historian-compare` verb, since neither side of a
historian-to-historian comparison is DeltaV-specific.

Also: the window now registers its own Windows taskbar identity (AppUserModelID), so it groups and shows its own icon on the taskbar instead of a generic one.

# v4
The quality column was inverted — every good sample was flagged bad

The sample list tested `status != 0` to decide whether to highlight a row. Quality
lives in the top two bits of the DeltaV status byte, so a good sample is 0x80–0xFF
and only 0x00 passed that test. The result was backwards: every GOODCASCADE and
GOODNONCASCADE sample was highlighted as bad, and the one genuinely bad byte
(0x00, BAD/non-specific) was shown as fine.

The status byte is now decoded through `shared.deltav.status` rather than guessed
at. Samples carry readable Quality, Substatus and Limit, the list highlights only
what is actually not-good, and the read summary says how many samples were not
good. The CSV export gains `quality`, `substatus`, `limit` and `is_good` columns
alongside the raw bytes, which are unchanged.

`archive_status` (holes, manual edits) is still exported raw — those flag
meanings are not yet documented.

# v27

A rebuild; the tool itself behaves as described under v25.

- **No new behaviour in this release.** The pattern warnings, the "0 matches" explanations and the write-time checks described under v25 are all in this build.

# v25

- **Replacing a whole expression now works.** Collapsing an expression onto a single tag, re-shaping one
  (dropping some terms and adding others), and changing an `and` to an `or` where that changes the order the
  picture evaluates in — none of these could ever be written. Each was routed to an engine that built the
  edit, and a check at the very end refused it; because that check refuses the WHOLE picture, one awkward
  expression meant nothing in the file was written. Measured before: 0 of 8. Now every one of them applies,
  and the finished file is re-read to prove it.
  - The message you would have seen was *"N expression(s) would ship unreadable"* or *"N expression(s) would
    ship with N missing data-source connection(s)"*.
  - **No picture was ever damaged by this.** The refusal happened before anything was written. If a colleague
    ran Picture Repair on the file and it came back healthy, that was correct — the file was never the
    problem, the edit was. Both messages now say so.
  - Where a replacement needs a longer tag name than the picture has room for in that slot, that ONE
    expression is reported skipped with the reason, and the rest of the file is written as normal.
- **A new check that reads the finished picture before writing it.** Every earlier check inspected the edit
  in memory, and that is not the same thing as the file. An edit can look perfect in memory and still write a
  picture where fifteen expressions have operands with nothing driving them — the failure where an alarm
  colour reads correctly in the editor and simply never changes on screen. Every write is now re-read and its
  live-data connections compared against the original; if the edit made them worse, nothing is written.
- **"0 matches" now tells you WHY.** A pattern that finds nothing used to look identical whether
  the text is genuinely absent or the pattern is one clause away from right. The preview now
  works out how far the pattern DOES match and names the clause the picture stops agreeing with,
  with an example of the closest value it found. A 640-character alarm-colour pattern that
  reported nothing turned out to end in a `_CND_01/DEPRIORITIZE` clause that particular picture
  does not have — visible immediately now, where before it meant dumping every expression in the
  file by hand.
- **A replacement that DELETES tags now says which ones.** This is the quiet one. A greedy `(.*)`
  in the Find swallows whatever sits between the tokens you wrote, and if the replacement only
  writes `${1}` back, everything the wildcard ate is deleted. The rule looks like a rename and
  the preview row is 600 characters wide, so two alarm terms vanishing from the middle are
  invisible. Every preview row for an expression now names the tag references the rewrite would
  remove — whether it is applied or skipped.
  - Real case: a pattern naming `_TE_01`, `_TE_01B` and `_ZS_01` matched rooms that also read
    `_HT_01`, `_HT_01B` and `_ZS_02`, and would have dropped four of the five alarms each room
    monitors.
- **Removing a term from an expression now works.** It routed to the right engine and built the right token
  graph, but the shortened display string was moved in the process and the expression was left with no
  display text at all — so the whole-picture check refused the file. Every attempt to delete a term was
  refused; measured 0 of 6 before, 6 of 6 now. The display is rewritten in place, which is what the
  rename path has always done — both now share the one implementation.
- **The command-line tool now shows the same warnings as the GUI.** `operate-cli fr --regex`
  printed none of them: greedy wildcards, capture groups the replacement never reads, the
  `$1_TE_01` group-name trap, over-wide

It can also turn on the Customer No-AI Lock, which keeps every CornerStone tool on Axiom: local and deterministic, with nothing sent to the cloud.

# v11

The emulated plant's instruments now raise their own alarms, and the whole FAT process is built in.

- **AI and PID blocks compute their alarms.** HI_HI, HI, LO and LO_LO flags on PV, and a PID's DV_HI and DV_LO on PV minus SP, are worked out with hysteresis. Modules read these flags, and before this they stayed UNKNOWN, so alarm-driven logic never saw an alarm.
- **Configured ranges survive loading.** Where the export had configured a scale such as OUT_SCALE.EU100 = 10000 but the record itself was absent, the default 0-100 was written over it, which put 25 modules of one plant on the wrong range. A default no longer replaces a value that is already there.
- **Transmitters rest inside their band.** A percent-channel input is read as 0-100 whatever its XD_SCALE says, and a transmitter whose mid-scale would sit in an alarm band now rests in the part of the band its range can actually reach.
- **A new FAT test entry under Test.** Generate cases from the open export, run them on a fresh emulator and export the executed record in one dialog, with an AI Synthesize option (Axiom, local model, Copilot, Claude on your Claude Code login, or the rule engine). The same dialog is in DvTwin.
- **Block inspector: Trace.** A Trace button traces upstream logic and evaluates live interlocks with Axiom's E-Graph, and shows a message if the trace cannot be launched.
- **Step state is readable from outside.** Reading MODULE/STEP/ACTIVE or /TIME for a module chart, or for a composite chart such as EM/COMMAND_00002/S0100/ACTIVE, answers as a faceplate or OPC client would see it.
- **Comparing two exports.** Suggested name rules now come from the suite's shared matcher (the one DifFHX uses) and unit-bound phases are paired by class name. A signal that moves on every scan is reduced to where it set off, turned and came to rest rather than a row per scan, which had put 1,464 rows of a decaying temperature into one report.

# v10

A phase's unit parameters were its own parameters, which is to say nothing.

- **`'/SETUP_DONE.CV'` from phase logic is the unit's parameter.** DeltaV Batch resolves a
  module-relative reference in a phase to the *unit* the phase runs on when the phase has no
  parameter of that name -- it is how a phase sets `PS_SETUP`, clears `MKUP_CONC`, reads
  `EMPTY_LVL`, and locks its devices with `'//#FV_PROD#/OWNER_ID.CV' := '/UNIT_NAME.CV'`.
  The engine resolved every one of them to `UNIT/PHASE/NAME`, a key nothing owned, so they
  read UNKNOWN: `UNIT_NAME` had no value, no lock ever confirmed, every lock step sat out its
  30 s time-out and the harness stepped in, and the training course's unit parameters never
  moved. Measured on the course's answer key: `MAKEUP_SETUP`'s lock step took 31 s and left
  every `OWNER_ID` at `(None)`; it now takes one scan and leaves them at `TK100_BA`, with
  `SETUP_DONE` True and `PS_SETUP` Running at the end, and the student-versus-key comparison
  of that phase matches on all six commands with 168 events a side.
